Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette:
Amina was an 80-year-old African woman who had spent much of her adult life as a pastor’s wife and, in later years, as a clergy woman herself, speaking with quiet authority in her congregation and in her home. She came to treatment only after years of resisting it, and even now she spoke of herself as someone who should simply endure. That conviction began in earnest during the years when her family fled violence and lived as refugees, when the ordinary act of moving through public space could turn dangerous without warning. She remembered being packed into a bus with strangers, her children pressed close, when armed men stopped the vehicle and shouted orders. The smell of dust and sweat, the harsh voices, and the flash of weapons being held up in the air stayed with her. Ever since, riding a bus or seeing a weapon, or even something used like one, could pull her attention sharply back to that day. On those occasions she would feel herself beginning to detach, unreal and far away, and she came to believe that anything which unsettled her like that could not be safely faced.

When those moments were stirred up, Amina responded by shrinking her life. She avoided talking with others about the event or what followed, insisting that discussion would open a door she could not close. She wore concealing clothing, choosing loose layers even in warm weather, partly because she did not want to be noticed and partly because being seen too clearly made her feel vulnerable. She also avoided seeking medical or psychological help for years, telling herself that she had survived too much already to be undone by talking. That conviction that she should be able to handle it on her own kept drawing her back to the memory at the worst moments, as if her mind returned to it to prove how badly she had failed to keep herself safe. These habits brought temporary relief, but they also narrowed her world and made every appearance of the old fear feel more important. A bus passing the church caught her attention for hours afterward; a glint of metal in someone’s hand at the grocery store could make her pull her scarf tighter and look away. When the world felt that dangerous, the memory came up more easily and more forcefully, surfacing in her mind as if she needed to keep revisiting the scene to stay alert for what might happen next. The more she avoided, the more certain she became that danger was close by, and she found herself watching other people closely for signs that they might harm her, especially if they made sudden movements. That constant effort to keep the fear at bay had the opposite effect on the memory itself: because she had spent so long not speaking of it or facing it directly, it remained raw and ready to break through, more vivid each time it returned. She frequently looked behind her when walking from the church lot to her car, afraid that someone might be following her.

Her understanding of what had happened also deepened the fear. Amina felt the event was deeply unfair and that nothing had ever been done about it. She said it had left her feeling like an object, not a person, carried along by other people’s decisions. That sense of injustice fed the belief that if she thought about it too directly she would not be able to handle it, so she kept trying to push it away. Yet the memory would not stay away on her terms. It forced its way into her mind when she did not want it to, often when she was already on edge. When that happened, she sometimes heard in her head the same shouted commands and rough voices she had heard during the frightening event, and the memory felt so extreme that it was hard for her to believe it had actually happened to her. The more sharply it intruded, the more she felt how unfair it had been and how reduced she had been to an object in the hands of others. That sense of humiliation and violation made the memory feel even more unbearable, and it sent her back toward silence, concealment, and vigilance.

Over time, those attempts to manage the fear kept the system alive rather than settling it. Because she stayed away from talking about the trauma, the memory remained fragmented and raw, more likely to break in without warning. Because she kept avoiding medical care, she had no opportunity to explain how the bus rides, the weapons, or the beginning of detachment were affecting her, and no one had helped her make sense of the fear. In her work and daily life, this was beginning to matter: she had stopped taking public transport to reach ministry commitments unless she had no other choice, and she shortened visits with congregants if someone moved too quickly around her. She had become known as polite but watchful, always scanning, always ready to leave. Her husband noticed that she startled at sudden movement and that she often turned to check behind her before settling anywhere. Amina herself felt trapped between the wish to remain composed and the constant pull of the old terror. She finally sought help after a bus ride to a church gathering left her trembling and unreal for the rest of the day, unable to concentrate on her sermon notes and ashamed that the memory had taken over again. What brought her in was not only the fear that she was becoming more frightened with age, but the fear that if she continued this way she would remain forever in the role the trauma had assigned her: watched, objectified, and unable to trust her own mind.

violations.explanation: The vignette never clearly shows that her negative appraisals drive the intrusive memory; it says the appraisals increase fear and avoidance, but not that they cause the memory to intrude or recur.
The vignette shows threat leading to fear and vigilance, but it does not state that her sense of threat causes the memory to intrude or intensify.
The vignette shows avoidance keeping the memory fragmented and raw, but it does not explicitly convey that her maladaptive strategies lead to the memory itself worsening or intruding as a result.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette never clearly shows that her negative appraisals drive the intrusive memory; it says the appraisals increase fear and avoidance, but not that they cause the memory to intrude or recur.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette shows threat leading to fear and vigilance, but it does not state that her sense of threat causes the memory to intrude or intensify.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette shows avoidance keeping the memory fragmented and raw, but it does not explicitly convey that her maladaptive strategies lead to the memory itself worsening or intruding as a result.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
